title: Oscar and the Undertow
premise: Oscar Galloway has spent eleven years mailing postcards to a house that burned down, writing to his mother as if the fire never happened. When his sister Vera clears their late aunt's estate and finds a box of letters the mother wrote but never sent—letters naming who really caused the death Oscar was blamed for—the siblings must decide whether truth is worth what it will cost them. The family's silence, they learn, was not protection but an inheritance passed down like debt. In the end, Oscar stops sending postcards and instead reads one letter aloud at the mother's bedside, choosing a justice no court could grant: being believed before her memory goes.
about_author: Rosalind Crane is a former probate clerk from coastal Maine whose novels examine the paperwork families use to avoid each other. She writes in the off-season, in houses borrowed from strangers.

chapters.title: The Address That Burned
chapters.summary: Oscar's POV. We follow his ritual: buying postcards, writing to 14 Marsh Lane, dropping them in the box, watching them vanish into dead-letter limbo. His landlady assumes he's a widower; he lets her. The chapter establishes his tenancy of his own life—present tense, careful, small. Emotional beat: the eerie comfort of addressing someone who cannot answer.

chapters.title: What Vera Found Behind the Wardrobe
chapters.summary: Vera's POV. Clearing Aunt Dot's house, she finds a box of unsent letters in their mother's hand, dated after the accident that killed their cousin Danny—letters that contradict the story the family agreed to tell. She confronts Oscar with them. He refuses to read past the first page. Emotional beat: the shock of discovering silence was authored, not accidental.

chapters.title: Everyone Who Signed Nothing
chapters.summary: Alternating POVs. The siblings trace who knew what: Uncle Ray's hush money, the aunt's locked drawer, the mother's complicity in letting twelve-year-old Oscar carry the blame. As they press, relatives close ranks; Vera's marriage strains under her digging. Climax builds when they realize the mother, now fading into dementia, may be the only witness left. Emotional beat: grief curdling into fury.

chapters.title: Read It to Me
chapters.summary: Oscar's POV. At the care facility, the mother surfaces briefly from her fog and asks about the postcards she somehow knows he sends. Instead of answering, Oscar reads her own unsent letter aloud—the confession she wrote and buried. She weeps, says his name, says 'it wasn't you,' then slips away again. He mails nothing more. Emotional beat: justice arrives unenforceable but real, and Oscar finally owns his days.
